what: The Derivative Calculator finds the derivative of a function and shows the rules used, step by step: the power, product, quotient and chain rules, plus the standard derivatives of trigonometric, exponential and logarithmic functions.

It also finds second and higher derivatives, the slope and tangent line at a point, partial derivatives, and draws the function together with its derivative. Every answer is checked against a numerical derivative.
It is made for students learning calculus and anyone who needs a quick, reliable derivative. It runs in your browser.
uses: Compare your working with the steps and the final answer.
See which rule applies to each part of a function and in which order.
Get the slope and the tangent line equation at any point.
Get the second derivative for concavity and acceleration, up to the fifth.
Differentiate with respect to one letter while the others are treated as constants.
tutorial: Enter it with x, such as x^2 sin(x) or (x^2 + 1)/(x - 1). You can leave out * between a number and a letter: 3x means 3·x. Open How to type functions for the full list.
The variable is x by default; change it to t or y if needed. Choose First, Second or a higher derivative.
The derivative appears in standard maths notation. The You entered box shows how your input was read, so you can spot typing mistakes.
Each step names the rule, gives its formula and shows the derivative of that part. Indented steps belong to the step above them.
Type a value such as 2 or pi/4 in Value at x. You get f(x), the derivative there and the tangent line equation, also drawn on the graph.
The blue curve is f(x) and the dashed orange curve is the derivative. Zoom in or out to explore.
features: Sum, constant multiple, power, product, quotient, chain, exponential and logarithmic differentiation.
Trigonometric, inverse trigonometric, hyperbolic, exponential, logarithms in any base, roots and absolute value.
Like terms are combined and fractions tidied.
Every first-order result is compared with a numerical derivative at several points.
Slope and equation at any point, plus a graph.
Up to the fifth derivative; other letters are treated as constants.

example.title: Worked example: x² sin(x)
example.text: The product rule gives d/dx[u·v] = u′v + uv′ with u = x² and v = sin(x). The power rule gives u′ = 2x and the standard derivative gives v′ = cos(x). So f′(x) = x² cos(x) + 2x sin(x). At x = 1, f′(1) = cos 1 + 2 sin 1 ≈ 2.2232, and the tangent line is y = 2.2232x − 1.3818.

tips: Use brackets generously: sin(2x)^2 is different from sin((2x)^2).
log(x) means base 10 and ln(x) means natural log, as on most calculators. For another base write log(x, 2).
Write e^(2x), not e^2x, which means e² · x.
If a result looks different from your textbook, it may be the same function written another way. Compare values at a point, or check the graph.
For implicit differentiation, solve for y first if you can, or use a partial derivative.
problems: It says something is not understood
Check for symbols the tool does not use, such as = or ', and make sure multiplication between brackets is clear.
Higher derivatives of complicated functions grow quickly. The result is correct, but simplifying by hand may give a shorter form.
The value at a point says undefined
The function or its derivative does not exist there, for example ln(x) at x = 0.
The function may have no real values in the visible range, such as sqrt(x) for negative x. Zoom out or change the point.
